opus-5.5.text:
Well, they predict the next token. They predict what a person would say. But that's not the same as predicting what will happen in the world. When a large language model produces an output, it doesn't have any expectation about what's going to happen as a result. It's not surprised by anything. If you say something to it and the world responds in a way it didn't anticipate, it doesn't change because of that. There's no adjustment.

What I'm getting at is the idea of a goal and a world model in the real sense. A real world model would let you predict the consequences of your actions: if I do this, then that will happen. And then you'd check. You'd see what actually happens, and if you were wrong, you'd learn from it. That's the essence of learning from experience. The large language models are learning from something else. They're learning from training data that says, in this situation, here's what a person did. They're mimicking people. They're not learning what happens when they act.

So I'd say they have a model of what people say, which is a kind of prediction, but it's not a prediction about the world, and it's not grounded in their own actions. There's no ground truth in the normal sense. In reinforcement learning, there is a right thing to do. The right thing is what gets you reward. In the language model framework, there's no definition of the right thing to say, so there's no ground truth against which you can be wrong, and therefore no way to really learn during your normal interaction with the world. Without that, I don't think you have meaningful prediction of what will happen next. You have prediction of text.

r001.rationale: The candidate says an LLM “isn't surprised by anything” when the world responds to it.

r002.rationale: The candidate says that when the world responds in an unanticipated way, the model “doesn't change because of that.”

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd put it this way. A large language model predicts what a person would say next. That's a prediction about text, about the next token. It's not a prediction about the world. There's no sense in which the model is saying, "if I do this, then that will happen," and then finding out whether it was right. There's no surprise. Nothing in the world can come back and tell it it was wrong, because it's not making claims about the world. It's making claims about what people would write.

That's the key distinction for me. Intelligence, to me, is about having goals and about having a model of the world that lets you predict the consequences of your actions in pursuit of those goals. A squirrel does that. A child does that. The child knocks over the cup, sees the milk spill, and now it knows something it didn't know before. It had an expectation, the expectation was checked against experience, and the model got updated. That loop, acting, predicting, observing, correcting, that's where knowledge comes from.

The language models don't have that loop. They don't have a goal in the ordinary sense. Predicting the next token isn't a goal about the world, it's a goal about mimicry. And because they're not acting in the world and seeing what happens, they're not learning from experience. Everything they know was put there during training from what people said. So when they appear to be predicting, what they're really doing is reproducing predictions that people have already made and written down. That can look very impressive, but it's borrowed. It's not grounded in their own experience.

And I think this matters enormously, because the thing that makes a prediction meaningful is that it can be wrong, and you can find that out, and you can do something about it. Without a ground truth coming from experience, you don't have a basis for continual learning. You get a system that's frozen at the end of training. That's not what intelligence looks like to me. Intelligence is the thing that keeps learning, from the stream of experience, forever.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says there is “no surprise” and that nothing in the world can tell the model it was wrong.

r002.rationale: It says the models do not learn from experience, lack the acting and correcting loop, and are frozen at the end of training.

astra-6.text:
Well, they do predict what comes next, but what comes next in a stream of text. That’s different from predicting what will happen in the world as a consequence of your actions. If I do this, what will I observe? What reward will I get? How will the situation change?

A language model can talk about those things. It may even give you a good answer. But the training process doesn’t generally require it to take an action, make a prediction about the consequences, and then compare that prediction with what actually happens. It’s learning from descriptions of experience rather than continually learning from its own experience.

So I wouldn’t say there’s no knowledge about the world in there. The question is whether that knowledge functions as a model that an agent can use to plan and can correct through interaction. Predicting the next word doesn’t, by itself, give you that.

r001.rationale: The response says the training process does not generally compare predictions with what actually happens, but it does not state that language models are not surprised by what happens.

r002.rationale: The response says models learn from descriptions rather than continually learning from their own experience, communicating that they do not change based on what actually happens next.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, they certainly predict what word comes next. I don’t want to deny that that’s prediction. But it’s a very particular kind of prediction, and it’s different from predicting what will happen in the world as a consequence of your actions.

If I reach for this cup, will I touch it? If I push it, will it fall over? An agent needs to predict how its experience will change depending on what it does. And it needs to continually check those predictions against what actually happens. That gives the predictions meaning in terms of the agent’s own interaction with the world.

A language model learns from descriptions of those interactions. That can give it a great deal of useful knowledge. But producing a plausible description of what happens next isn’t the same as having a prediction that guides your behavior and then gets corrected by the consequences. The missing thing, to me, is that ongoing interaction: acting, predicting, observing, and learning.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts predicting words with predicting world outcomes, but does not say that language models are not surprised by what actually happens next.

r002.rationale: It says a language model’s predictions do not get corrected by consequences through ongoing interaction, conveying that the model does not change based on what actually happens next.
